title: Can, must, may, and must not
title_target: ໄດ້ ຕ້ອງ ຄວນ ຫ້າມ — Dâi, tâwng, khuan, hàam
goal: Ask permission, say what's required, give advice, and understand prohibitions — four things that decide whether you sound polite or like you're giving orders.

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — Temple rules, before going in
dialogs.intro: Bounmy explains the rules before they enter the wat. Notice how strict prohibitions and gentle advice use different words.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ກ່ອນ|Kàwn][ເຂົ້າ|khào] [ຕ້ອງ|tâwng][ຖອດ|thàwt][ເກີບ|kòep][ເດີ້|dòe]
lines.id: Before going in, you have to take off your shoes, okay?
lines.literal: before — enter — must — remove — shoe — (friendly particle).

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ເຂົ້າໃຈ|Khào-jai][ແລ້ວ|lèeo] [ຖ່າຍ|Thàai][ຮູບ|hûup][ໄດ້|dâi][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Got it. Can I take photos?

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ຖ່າຍ|Thàai][ຢູ່|yùu][ນອກ|nàwk][ໄດ້|dâi] [ແຕ່|Tèe][ຢູ່|yùu][ໃນ|nai][ຫ້າມ|hàam][ຖ່າຍ|thàai] [ມີ|Míi][ປ້າຍ|pâai][ຂຽນ|khǐan][ໄວ້|wâi]
lines.id: Outside, yes. But inside it's forbidden. There's a sign that says so.
lines.literal: take — at — outside — can. but — at — inside — forbid — take. have — sign — write — keep.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ໃສ່|sài][ໂສ້ງ|sôong][ຂາ|khǎa][ສັ້ນ|sân] [ເປັນ|Pen][ຫຍັງ|nyǎng][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: I'm wearing shorts. Is that a problem?
lines.literal: I — wear — pants — leg — short. be — what — (question)?

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ບໍ່|Bàw][ຄວນ|khuan][ເດີ້|dòe] [ຕ້ອງ|Tâwng][ປົກ|pók][ຫົວ|hǔa][ເຂົ່າ|khào] [ຢືມ|Yʉʉm][ຜ້າ|phàa][ຢູ່|yùu][ທາງ|tháang][ເຂົ້າ|khào][ໄດ້|dâi]
lines.id: Better not. You need to cover your knees. You can borrow a cloth at the entrance.
lines.literal: not — should — (friendly particle). must — cover — knee. borrow — cloth — at — way — enter — can.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ດີ|Dii] [ຕ້ອງ|Tâwng][ຈ່າຍ|jàai][ຄ່າ|khàa][ເຂົ້າ|khào][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Okay. Do I have to pay an entrance fee?

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ບໍ່|Bàw][ຈຳເປັນ|jam-pen] [ແຕ່|Tèe][ຖ້າ|thàa][ຢາກ|yàak][ບໍລິຈາກ|baw-li-jàak] [ກໍ|kaw][ໄດ້|dâi]
lines.id: No need. But if you want to make a donation, that's fine.
lines.literal: not — necessary. but — if — want — donate — also — can.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ບໍ່|bàw][ຮູ້|hûu][ຈັກ|ják][ວິທີ|wi-thíi][ໄຫວ້|wâi] [ຊ່ວຍ|Sùay][ສອນ|sǎwn][ແດ່|dèe][ໄດ້|dâi][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: I don't know how to do the wai. Could you show me?
lines.literal: I — not — know — method — wai. help — teach — a-little — can — (question)?

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi][ເລີຍ|lóei] [ເອົາ|Ao][ມື|mʉʉ][ສອງ|sǎwng][ຂ້າງ|khàang][ປະ|pa][ກັນ|kan] [ແລ້ວ|Lèeo][ກໍ|kaw][ກົ້ມ|kôm][ຫົວ|hǔa][ໜ້ອຍ|nàwy][ໜຶ່ງ|nʉ̀ng]
lines.id: Sure. Press both hands together, then bow your head a little.
lines.literal: can — right-away. take — hand — two — side — press — together. then — also — bow — head — little — one.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ແບບ|Bèep][ນີ້|nîi][ບໍ່|bàw] [ຖືກ|Thʉ̀ʉk][ບໍ່|bàw]

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ຖືກ|Thʉ̀ʉk][ແລ້ວ|lèeo] [ເກັ່ງ|Kèng][ຫຼາຍ|lǎai] [ໄປ|Pai][ກັນ|kan][ເລີຍ|lóei]
lines.id: That's right. Well done. Let's go in.
lines.literal: correct — already. skilled — much. go — together — right-away.

notes: **Two words for "can", and this is what separates advanced speakers.** *ໄດ້ dâi* = able, allowed, have the chance — used for permission and possibility. *ເປັນ pen* = can because you've learned how — used for skills. *ຖ່າຍຮູບໄດ້ບໍ່* (may I take photos?) versus *ຖ່າຍຮູບເປັນບໍ່* (can you take photos? — do you have the skill?).

**ຕ້ອງ tâwng = "must", and its negative ບໍ່ຕ້ອງ does NOT mean "don't have to".** *ບໍ່ຕ້ອງ bàw tâwng* means "no need, don't bother" — an offer to spare you trouble. For "not required", the word is *ບໍ່ຈຳເປັນ bàw jam-pen*.

**ຄວນ khuan = "should", ບໍ່ຄວນ = "shouldn't".** It's advice, not an order, and Lao people use it far more often than *ຕ້ອງ*. Saying *ບໍ່ຄວນ* to a foreigner about to break a custom is the gentlest way to stop them — and that's what you hear in this dialog.

**ຫ້າມ hàam = "forbidden", and it's the official word.** It's what's written on signs: *ຫ້າມຖ່າຍຮູບ* (no photography), *ຫ້າມສູບຢາ* (no smoking), *ຫ້າມຈອດ* (no parking). Whenever you see this word on a sign, stop and find out what it says.

**ຢ່າ yàa = "don't", used from person to person.** *ຢ່າໄປ* (don't go). The difference from *ຫ້າມ*: *ຫ້າມ* is a rule, *ຢ່າ* is a personal request. Adding *ເດີ້* at the end softens it: *ຢ່າລືມເດີ້* (don't forget, okay).

**ຊ່ວຍ… ແດ່ sùay… dèe is the most polite frame for asking a favor.** *ຊ່ວຍສອນແດ່* (please teach me), *ຊ່ວຍເປີດປະຕູແດ່* (please open the door), *ຊ່ວຍເວົ້າຊ້າໆແດ່* (please speak slowly). The two words wrap around the verb, and without them your sentence is an order.

**ຮູ້ຈັກ hûu-ják = "know (a person), know how", ຮູ້ hûu = "know (a fact)".** *ຂ້ອຍບໍ່ຮູ້* (I don't know), *ຂ້ອຍບໍ່ຮູ້ຈັກລາວ* (I don't know him). For knowing how to do something, people use *ຮູ້ຈັກວິທີ* or simply *ເຮັດບໍ່ເປັນ* (can't do it).

**ໄຫວ້ wâi is the pressed-palms gesture of respect, and its height has rules.** To peers: fingertips at chin level. To elders and teachers: at the nose. To monks and Buddha images: at the forehead. The younger person goes first; the elder returns it. When in doubt, copy the person next to you.

**Ten unwritten temple rules.** Take off your shoes, cover shoulders and knees, don't point your feet at a Buddha image, sit with your legs folded back away from the image, don't stand higher than a monk, women must not touch monks, don't speak loudly, don't photograph people praying, don't climb on images for photos, and don't hand money directly to a monk.

grammars.title: Four helping verbs and their negatives
after: Notice the position: *ໄດ້*, *ເປັນ*, and *ໄຫວ* come **after** the verb; *ຕ້ອງ*, *ຄວນ*, *ຫ້າມ*, and *ຢ່າ* come **before** it. That's the only thing to memorize — the rest follows naturally.
**ໄຫວ *wǎi*** means "physically able to". *ຍ່າງບໍ່ໄຫວ* (can't walk any more), *ກິນບໍ່ໄຫວ* (can't eat another bite). A very useful word when you're truly exhausted.

blocks.text: The last two words are worth learning by heart: **ຊາຍ *sáai*** (men) and **ຍິງ *nyíng*** (women). In many places, that's the only marking on a restroom door — no pictures.

sections.title: Customs to know before you get them wrong

head: Don't
Why
Instead
rows: the head is considered most sacred
the left hand is for unclean things
right hand, left hand supporting the elbow
shoot from a distance, no flash
place the item on a cloth
bow your head as you pass

blocks.text: One principle explains almost every row in this table: in Lao culture, **high means honored and low means less honored** — literally. The head is up, the feet are down, and every movement of the body carries that meaning. Understand this one principle and you can guess the rest yourself.

The second principle: **ບໍ່ເສຍໜ້າ bàw sǐa nâa** — don't make people lose face. Scolding someone in front of others, pushing for a firm answer, or showing anger will cost you far more than the problem you're trying to solve. What works in Laos is almost always a smile, patience, and calmly repeating your request.
